The logical principle (*nyāya*), however, is as follows—this being the distinction: if the witness fails to state the number at all, or states a higher number, then a different procedure applies to the entire claim (*pratijñā*) itself; for since that witness is mistaken regarding the number, it is possible he is also mistaken regarding the substance, and thus his testimony is not even accepted. In the case of stating a lower number, if the mention of "fifty" is rooted in error or the like, there is no ground for suspicion; however, if he has failed to mention what is in excess, forgetfulness is suspected. Since fallacies such as quibbling (*chala*) must be rejected in legal proceedings (*dharmavyavahāra*), the failure to state "fifty" is taken up because there is no contradiction or similar defect, and thus it is examined for corroboration. Furthermore, one should not resort to other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) here merely because something was not stated, and so forth. Once this [witness] has passed the test of examination, other means of knowledge are useless. It must be discerned that there is no further determination regarding anything beyond the fifty *purāṇas* mentioned by the witness.

As for that which was stated by Nārada regarding the liability to pay the entire subject matter of a dispute even when only a portion has been proven, it is as follows: "When one who is accused on multiple counts denies the entire matter, yet a single part is proven, it is proper that even that [entirety] be paid. [N?]

Therefore, this [rule] regarding the mention of "one" (eka) must be explained as referring to cases where the mention of one is invariably concomitant with the mention of others, due to the contradiction with many other statements. For example: when a thief has seized a vessel containing various items such as gold and so forth, if even a single part—namely, any one of those items like gold—is recovered, then the entire [stolen property] must be returned. Thus, the term "one part" (ekadeśa) refers to a part that is pervading [the whole], because this statement is rooted in logic (*nyāya*). Alternatively, it concerns the matter of royal punishment. This was stated by Yājñavalkya: *YDh 2.167:* *anekārthābhiyoge tu yāvat saṃsādhayed dhanī |* *sādhite 'rthe 'rthasaṃbandhe grāhyas tv ekadeśataḥ ||* "But when there is an accusation involving multiple objects, however much the creditor may prove; once the object is proven and the connection with the debt is established, he may be made to accept [payment] from a single part. *YDh 2.170:* *na ca mithyābhiśasto 'sau mucyate daṇḍam arhati |* *mithyābhiśaṃsī ca tathā yathā pāpam abhiśastaḥ ||* "And he who is falsely accused is not released; he deserves punishment, as does the one who makes a false accusation, according to the nature of the crime committed by the accused. *YDh 2.171:* *yo naiva divyena na mānuṣeṇa saṃsādhayed artham uttamaṃ ca |* *rājñā svakośād dātavyo grāhyas tasmāc ca sodhyaḥ ||* "He who cannot recover his own property or the debt owed to him through either divine or human means, should have it paid by the king from his own treasury, and he [the debtor] should be made to pay it back to him. *YDh 2.173:* *na dadāti hi yaḥ śakto yo 'rthitve sati vastuni |* *sa nigṛhya balād dāpyo daṇḍyaś caiva na dāpayet ||* "For he who, being capable, does not give when there is a request for a thing, should be seized by force and compelled to give; otherwise, he should be fined and not made to pay. *YDh 2.180:* *yo yāvan nihnuvītārthaṃ mithyā yāvati vā vadet |* *tau nṛpeṇa hy adharmajñau dāpyau taddviguṇaṃ damam ||* "To whatever extent a person denies a claim, or to whatever extent he speaks falsely, both of them, being ignorant of dharma, shall be made by the king to pay double that amount as a fine. *YDh 2.194:* *na dadāti hi yaḥ śakto dhanaṃ daṇḍaṃ ca rājani |* *sa kūṭasākṣiṇāṃ pāpaistulyadoṣo bhṛgoḥ kule ||* "For he who, being capable, does not pay the wealth or the fine to the king, possesses a fault equal to that of false witnesses; [this is the law] in the lineage of Bhṛgu. *YDh 2.195:* *yo 'rthinam artham āhūya paścān naiva prayacchati |* *sa nigṛhya balād dāpyo daṇḍyaś caiva na dāpayet ||* "He who, having summoned a plaintiff for his cause, subsequently does not deliver it, should be seized by force and compelled to pay; otherwise, he should be fined and not made to pay. *YDh 2.196:* *arthe 'pavyayamānaṃ tu karaṇena vibhāvitam |* *dāpayed dhanikasyārthaṃ daṇḍaleśaṃ ca śaktitaḥ ||* "But one who denies a claim, when it is proved by evidence, the king shall compel him to pay the debt to the creditor and a small portion of a fine according to his capacity. *YDh 2.197:* *nikṣepopanidhiyācitāvakrītādhayo nṛṇām |* *naṣṭā naṣṭā na dāpyāḥ syur akāle yadi tān vinā ||* "If the deposits, open deposits, borrowed goods, purchases, and pledges of men are lost without those [deposits etc. being present, they should not be made to pay for the loss if it occurred at the improper time. *YDh 2.198:* *vikrayaṃ vā krayaṃ vāpi nikṣepe yadi kurvate |* *na tatra kāraṇaṃ jñeyaṃ nikṣeptā cet svaṃ nāśayet ||* "If they [the depositors] engage in sale or purchase regarding a deposit, no blame is to be attributed to them, provided the depositor himself loses his own property. *YDh 2.199:* *svayam eva tu yo dadyān mṛtasya pratyanantare |* *na sa rājñābhiyoktavyo na nikṣeptuś ca bandhubhiḥ ||* "But he who gives [the deposit] himself to the heir of the deceased should not be prosecuted by the king nor by the relatives of the depositor. *YDh 2.200:* *grāhakair gṛhīte dravye naṣṭe moṣe ca kāraṇam |* *vikrayaṃ vā krayaṃ vāpi darśayeyuḥ parādhinaḥ ||* "When a commodity is seized by robbers, or lost in a robbery, those dependent on others [the owners] should show the cause, whether it be a sale or a purchase. *YDh 2.201:* *moṣe tu sahasā dattvā hīnakālaṃ parādhinaḥ |* *paścād avagame dāpyāḥ prathamāṃ sāhasaṃ damam ||* "But in the case of a robbery, if those dependent on others give [the value] immediately, yet later discover [the theft], they should be made to pay the first amercement. *YDh 2.202:* *vikretādarśayann arthaṃ krayam ādāya tiṣṭhati |* *hīnakālaṃ tu yo bhuṅkte sa tam arthaṃ pradāpyate ||* "If a seller, having taken the price, remains without showing the object, or if one enjoys it after the time limit has expired, he is made to pay that object. *YDh 2.203:* *yo darśayati nātmīyaṃ hīnakālaṃ ca yaḥ krayam |* *na sa taṃ labhate 'rthaṃ tu dāpyaś caitāvato damam ||* "He who does not show his own [property], or he who makes a purchase at an improper time, does not recover that object, and he must be made to pay a fine of that same amount. *YDh 2.204:* *dravyam ādāya yo mohād anyasmai pratipādayet |* *ādāya dāpitas taṃ tu daṇḍyaḥ syāc caurakilbiṣam ||* "He who, out of delusion, hands over a commodity after taking it [from another], having been made to pay it back, should be punished with the penalty for theft. *YDh 2.205:* *pratigrahe kraye vāpi

430. If a dispute should be accompanied by a wager (*paṇa*), the judge shall cause the loser to pay that wager, as well as a fine, and the debt itself to the creditor. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.18) The meaning of "wager" (*paṇa*) here refers to a case where one has stipulated, for instance, "I must pay everything even if only a single part is proven against me. Because of the use of the word "own" (*sva*) in this context, it should be understood that a wager made by another person need not be paid by the other party.

The *Mitākṣarā* states that when a witness declares either less or more than [the truth], there is a different legal procedure even regarding the substance of the claim. Furthermore, when a witness, being questioned about the matter asserted in the plaint, does not state that very matter but rather something subsumed under it, in that case as well, there is victory for the plaintiff alone; for by means of the inference established by his statement, the matter asserted by the plaintiff is proven. Nor should it be argued that this is not so because the witness did not state that specific point.
"He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor" (Vi 8.38ab).

Since this legal tradition (*smṛti*) is rooted in reason (*nyāya*), the term "witnesses" (*sākṣin*) is used figuratively; thus, the meaning is that whoever has proven their asserted matter by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the victor.
Furthermore, when even a portion of the matter to be proved (*sādhyārtha*) has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case is considered won.

"Whatever is prescribed as the penalty for association with women, for acts of violence, and for theft," according to this statement by Kātyāyana; thus, the *Mitākṣarā* states that full liability arises even when only a portion of the property is stolen in cases such as theft.

However, where a witness who has heard [the matter] says upon being questioned, "I heard this matter [from someone else]," there is no establishment of the fact, because there is no necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) between a word and its object. Rather, just as from perception, one determines the object even from a word; in that case, when the matter is known through a word untainted by the stain of doubt regarding its validity, and the witness states that very matter exactly as it was declared, only then is there the establishment of the fact. But if there is such a stain, he is not a witness, nor is his declaration to be accepted.
Regarding the conflict of statements among witnesses who have been questioned, Manu says:

In a conflict of witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; when they are equal in number, those superior in qualities; and when there is a conflict between those of equal qualities, the best among the twice-born. "Conflict" (*dvaidha*) refers here to the statement of something contrary to what was said by other witnesses. Thus, even in the case of stating "I do not know," there is no conflict, because that statement pertains to the absence of knowledge and does not touch upon the absence of the object to be known. Regarding the phrase "when they are equal": the meaning is that when there is equality in number, those with superior qualities should be accepted; when there is equality in qualities, those superior in caste (*jāti*) should be accepted. The implication is that when there is total equality in all respects, one must resort to other means of proof (*mānāntara*).
Nārada: In case of a conflict among witnesses, many are considered authoritative;
if they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; if they are equal in purity, those with better memories should be accepted.
Contradiction (*vipratipatti*) is the statement of two parties regarding mutually opposed existence and non-existence.
Yājñavalkya (4.35): "Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if there are others who possess greater [qualifications],"
Or if they should state it otherwise as being double, the former witnesses would be considered fraudulent. Kātyāyana also says:
"When the matter stated by the witnesses comes to be [contradicted] by the litigants..."
When the defendant there produces evidence to the contrary,
or when the previous witnesses are shown to be fraudulent by reason of their being numerous or of noble birth, they are deemed false;
"false" means their testimony is not to be accepted.
Now, it may be objected:
"He who, having abandoned a strong means of proof, resorts to a weak one, shall not regain that means of proof once the case has been decided by the members of the court. [K 221]

If it is asked how the acceptance of witnesses and other evidence that is "twofold" (dviguṇa) can be consistent with this contradiction from Kātyāyana, [the answer is]: because of the qualification "he is determined to have won," this statement refers to a situation subsequent to the determination of victory. Furthermore, the general statements of Yājñavalkya and others pertain to a state where victory has not yet been determined. The word *tyaktvā* means "without having produced. Therefore, even if a stronger proof has not been produced previously, once a weaker proof has been introduced, that stronger proof must indeed be employed during the stage of doubt, even if it is produced later. For this very reason, the author of the Ratnākara has recorded as established practice that a stronger alternative proof may be accepted within seven days, and even beyond that period.
Nārada: For those whose legal disputes have been adjudicated, the evidence—whether documentary or testimonial—is rendered fruitless if it was not previously presented. [NMā 1.62]

"Previously" means: where the strong evidence—such as witnesses and so forth—which was previously presented by the plaintiff, could not be employed due to defects such as distance, and which was disregarded by the judge under the delusion that it was impossible to employ; in such a case, even after seven days have passed, if that strong evidence is subsequently produced, it must be employed again. And this "re-examination" arises from the defect of a delusion regarding that strong evidence, which is capable of being employed, being taken to be incapable of being employed. As it has been said:
"Upon the refutation of witnesses, assessors, or those who have fallen away, there is a re-examination.
This applies in the same way to lamps and other such things. Now, as for what is written:
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Since confusion may arise even regarding a six-month period,
the Creator created letters long ago so that they might be inscribed upon leaves."
Nārada:

441. Documentary evidence is said to be of two kinds: that written in one's own hand and that written by another; it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of both depends upon their established usage in the particular region.

The meaning is that a document written by oneself is authoritative even without relying on witnesses, whereas one written by another is authoritative only by relying on them. Furthermore, that [document] is of six kinds, distinguished as: debt, sale, partition, gift, settlement, and deed of victory (*jaya-pattra*). A deed of gift (*dāna-pattra*) is also twofold, distinguished as being by a non-king or by a king. And each of these six types is further twofold, according to whether it is valid or invalid.
Yājñavalkya:

442. Even without witnesses, a document written in one’s own hand is declared to be valid in all cases, except when it was produced by force or through fraud (*upādhi*). Regarding the phrase "in one’s own hand": the meaning is that which was written by the very person who is the defendant (*abhiyojya*) based on the validity of that document. The term "force" (*bala*) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all defects that cause invalidity, such as pain, passion, hatred, fear, minority, and so forth.
In the second [section], Nārada says:
"The witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers and so forth, should write: 'I, so-and-so, am a witness here'; thus they are equal. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.87)
In the teaching [of Yājñavalkya], however:
"Having given land or having established a fixed endowment (nibandha), the king should cause a document to be prepared;
therein, for the information of future kings... (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.318).
On cloth or on a copper plate, marked with one's own seal; a *nibandha* is that which is to be held as fixed by its form and so forth. A *jayapatra*, however, has been described previously.

If there is a doubt regarding the invalidity of a document, it must be refuted by the holder of that document. However, his son need only present possession as proof of the document's validity; he is not required to produce the document itself. As Kātyāyana states:
"The claimant, even if he possesses possession, must clear the document of defects. His son, however, must clear possession of defects, but he shall not be required to produce the document. (K 323)
Bṛhaspati: The claimant shall remove the document; his son, however, shall remove only the possession.
If the one who was sued has died, his son too shall remove that [document].

Regarding the term "one who is charged" (*abhiyukta*): the meaning is that when the holder of a document has died without having informed his son, and the matter of the document's validity is to be established by that son, he is considered "charged" for the purpose of ascertaining the correctness of the writing.
Kātyāyana says: "If the debtor, upon seeing the document, does not clearly state its defect..."

Then, after twenty years have passed, the document shall become stable. When the wealth of one who is capable is enjoyed through a written document for as long as twenty years, that document is free from defect.
Now, regarding the weakness of documentary evidence: on this point, Vyāsa states—450.
A document that has not been seen or read out, or one where the creditor or debtor is deceased;
"Furthermore, a document that lacks a pledge or a surety does not become valid for a long time.
(Vy 1.69) The meaning is that a document is not authoritative when it relies on the seven defects, such as "not being shown" and so forth.
Bṛhaspati states an exception to this:

451. For those who are insane, dull-witted, or children; for those living abroad out of fear of the king; and for those who are timid or afflicted by fear, a document shall not suffer loss [of validity].
The meaning is that a document belonging to such persons as the insane and others does not incur invalidity merely because it was not shown [to the debtor] or similar reasons.
Now, possession (*bhukti*). Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"Possession that is accompanied by title, long-standing, uninterrupted, and free from any rival claim..."

And possession (*bhoga*) is held to be fivefold when accompanied by the presence of the opponent; "is a means of proof" is the ellipsis. *Āgama* is that by which [property] comes into one's own possession, such as purchase and so forth; it is "possessed of that. It is "of long duration," meaning its time is not less than the period prescribed by tradition (*smṛti*). It is "uninterrupted," meaning continuous. It is "free from blemish," meaning devoid of any manifestation of a contrary claim by another. It is "in the presence of the opponent," meaning occurring where the defendant or the other party is present. [Objection: But is being "accompanied by title" (*sāgamatva*) redundant? For even possession devoid of that is authoritative. To this, Nārada says:
453. But that which was enjoyed through unjust means by a father and three preceding ancestors cannot be overturned, having been acquired through succession over three generations. 454.
That which was previously enjoyed by three predecessors even without a legal title—
That which has been enjoyed for three successive generations cannot be overturned, even in the absence of a title deed.
Vyāsa says: "That which has been enjoyed for an extremely long time by three preceding ancestors, without a title deed..."
That which has been inherited through three generations cannot be set aside.
Vyāsa says that it is enjoyed for three generations:
"That which was enjoyed by the grandfather, and by his son in his absence..."
"Without those two, the enjoyment of one by whom they were given by the father belongs to three generations.
[Vy 1.83] Because there is no fixed rule regarding the lifespan of men, he himself defines "enjoyment by a man":
"Having enjoyed it for twenty years, while it remains unchallenged by the owner..."
"Enjoyment for one generation from the land is *pauruṣī*; twice that is *dvipuruṣī*, and thrice that is *tripuruṣī*; in these cases, there is no need to consider the title-deed (*āgama*).

[Vyāsa 1.81] And thus, it is not the case that enjoyment for three generations is a valid means of proof independently of a title-deed, because it contradicts another statement. To this effect, Viṣṇu says:
But when possession has been properly enjoyed for a period accompanied by title, the acquirer obtains it there; it can never be taken away from him.
"Acquirer" means the possessor. "Can be taken away" refers to the owner of that property.

459. But regarding property that was enjoyed by the father in accordance with custom and according to dharma—when he has died, no blame should be attached to him, for having enjoyed it, it rightfully became his. 460.
Furthermore, land that has been enjoyed by three successive generations of men in accordance with the prescribed rule...

"Even in the absence of a written document, one may obtain that [title] there as the fourth [means], by means of possession (bhukti) characterized by its being unbroken and so forth; that is to say, according to rule, by one who is capable and present, provided there is no contradiction or the like. — Yājñavalkya.
461. Possession acquires the status of valid proof through a pure title; possession with an impure title never attains validity. Nārada also says:
"But the king should punish that sinner who enjoys property without title for many hundreds of years with the punishment due to a thief.

[N 1.87] [Objection: "Alas! Because of this contradiction, let there simply be doubt. [Response: No, because the subject matter (*viṣaya*) differs. For the former statements proceed by taking possession (*āgama*) as the basis for doubt, whereas the latter proceed by taking it as the basis for the certainty of its existence. Thus, it is established that in a case where possession has lasted for three generations, enjoyment (*bhoga*) is a means of proof even when there is doubt regarding title; however, in other cases, it is a means of proof only when accompanied by certainty of title.
Yājñavalkya (2.24): There is loss of ownership after twenty years of land being enjoyed by another while one sees it and remains silent; for wealth, the loss occurs after ten years.
Of wealth, such as cattle and the like;
[thus says] Bṛhaspati:
"From the time of initial occupation, the possession of one that remains uninterrupted..."
"One should not displace him from that possession which has been uninterrupted for thirty years.
[B 7.28] "Adhyāsana" refers to acquisition through purchase and other such means.

Now, is there not a mutual contradiction between these two statements? For, by asserting the validity of possession for thirty years, the validity of possession for twenty years is effectively excluded.

No; for since the text states "one who sees but does not speak," where there is not even a mere word of contradiction, possession for twenty years alone is the proof. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement that "possession for thirty years is unimpeded," the meaning of the term "impediment" is restricted to quarrels, physical assault, and the like; thus, even if there is a disagreement consisting of mere words, possession for thirty years remains a valid proof of ownership of land. Consequently, by these two statements, possession for ten years in the case of cattle and other such things is authoritative, as is possession for twenty years in the case of land; likewise, in the case of land specifically, possession for thirty years—even if accompanied by [minor] noise—is authoritative provided it is free from quarrels and the like.

How, then, is it said that this [possession] is authoritative only in the case of three generations? Regarding this, Ratnākara states: "For the statement of one who speaks is not a means of proof for ownership in the case of the enjoyer, but rather in other cases. For instance, the meaning is that from the side of such an enjoyer—one who possesses but does not speak—the owner of the cattle, land, or other property does not recover that wealth by virtue of its connection with his enjoyment.
"He who, out of delusion, neglects goods being enjoyed by others, even while seeing them in his presence—his possession renders those goods subject to the other's control. (N 1.78)

This is precisely the meaning of Nārada’s statement as well. However, the *Pradīpa* [interprets] the statement beginning with “of one who sees [the loss] but does not speak” (*paśyato ’bruvataḥ*) as referring to a case where the mortgagee’s failure to establish [ownership] results from his non-usage of the pledge. Thus, in a case where the mortgagee does not use the mortgaged land or other property, but rather the pledgor himself uses it for a long time and then mortgages it elsewhere, the subsequent mortgagee possesses sovereignty over that land and so forth, but not the first one. And so it is said:
“In the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the earlier [title] is indeed more powerful. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.23cd)

Although there is such a statement as this, nevertheless, for one who perceives that which sets aside [the general rule], there is the statement "of one who does not speak" and so forth. And thus, by the force of that exception, the pledge (*adhi*) belongs to the second alone. The detailed exposition (*prapañca*) is also like this.

Alternatively, this refers to the fact that for the examiner who remains indifferent toward such a ground for defeat (*hānipada*), there arises a doubt of an inferior degree; it does not mean that defeat is necessarily the same as a formal loss (*bhaṅga*). If that were the case, it would be inconsistent with statements established by tradition, such as: "In the absence of punishment, the defeated party may be made to appear again, and the debate is resumed," and so forth. Therefore, even in the face of such a defeat, a final determination must be reached through further deliberation. For this very reason it is said: "Just as a cow left unattended perishes without a herdsman..."
Likewise, land that has been enjoyed by others while one looks on is lost over time.
Even if land has been enjoyed by others here for twenty years,
it is not established as his property in this world if there is a capable king who can act.

Thus, disregarding the two statements of Vyāsa, it is explained even in the *Ratnākara* that "if the land of one is enjoyed by others, it is lost to him; it is no longer determined as his own. Furthermore, if twenty years of possession were a proof of ownership in and of themselves, then since the point to be proven would be established by that alone— "When a person who is capable [of contesting] possesses property that is enjoyed by means of a document for twenty years, that document is free from defect. (Kātyāyana 299)
Thus, by this statement of Kātyāyana, that which was asserted—that possession serves to refute defects in documentary evidence—would be contradicted.

In reality, however, the Smṛti texts concerning loss (hāni) are supplementary to the injunction regarding the duty of preserving one's means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that one's own means of proof must be preserved by all means and one must not remain indifferent toward it. For this very reason, after citing the passages on loss in the *Kalpataru*, the preservation of the means of proof is concluded. Yājñavalkya:

"Even scriptural title (*āgama*) is not a strength where possession (*bhukti*), however slight, is absent. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.27cd) The meaning is that even when a title exists, if there is an absence of enjoyment for that duration of time, the notion that ownership continues does not arise. Regarding the point where two litigants proceed by the force of their respective titles, and the priority between the two titles cannot be determined, the author of the *Mitākṣarā* explains that the meaning is: "In such a case, the title of the one who has possession is stronger than that of the other. Nārada says:
471. Even though a document exists and witnesses are still living, that which has not been enjoyed—especially in the case of immovable property—is not secure. Likewise:

472. However, through actual enjoyment, the property of an owner is lost after twenty years (*dvidaśāḥ samāḥ*). Even deposits and the like are forfeited, with the exception of the property of women and the king. "Twenty years" means twenty years. "With the exception of the property of women and the king" means excluding the property of women and royal wealth.
Manu:
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while he is present, yet remains silent, he is not entitled to recover it. (MDh 8.147)

"Ten years" refers to the maximum period for land and wealth. Gautama states: "The property of one who is not mentally incapacitated or a minor, if enjoyed by others in the presence of the owner for ten years, belongs to the enjoyer. [G 12.34]

*Jaḍaḥ* means a fool. *Pogaṇḍaḥ* refers to one whose age is under sixteen years; for it is stated in the legal texts: "A child is to be known as such until the sixteenth year, and he is called *pogaṇḍa*. And thus, according to the *Ratnākara* and other authorities, it is understood that when the wealth of a capable person is enjoyed by another in his presence, it generally belongs to the enjoyer.
Manu:
Both a pledge (ādhi) and a deposit (upanidhi) do not suffer by the lapse of time; yet both would be forfeited if they remain for an excessively long period. [M 8.145]

*Ādhi* means a pledge (*bandha*). *Upanidhi*, however, is that which is delivered out of affection for the purpose of enjoyment, such as a field and so forth; it is not defined by the Smṛti as "that which is deposited without being described" and the like, because that [latter kind] is unfit for enjoyment. "They do not suffer from the lapse of time" means that at the time of redemption, they must necessarily be released by the pledgor and the depositor. He states the reason for this with the words "they are liable to be taken away," and so forth. For if these two remain for a long period, they may become subject to appropriation by the enjoyer, and the enjoyer might even seize them. — Bṛhaspati.
477. Or, if property is given openly by others to someone while another person is already enjoying it, that latter person does not deserve to recover it.
478. He who, seeing another giving away land, does not object to it—
Even by means of a document, the owner shall not recover that property again.
Likewise:
"Non-enjoyment of land and the failure to produce a document at the proper time..."
Furthermore, the failure to recall [the facts] by witnesses leads to the loss of one's own case.
Therefore, one must take great care to preserve the means of proof;
by that, both immovable and movable legal matters are successfully resolved.

Regarding the phrase "by the heirs": when the wealth of an owner is given by his heirs or others for the sake of another person, even in the very presence of that owner, the original owner does not recover that property from the recipient who is using it. In such a case, the meaning is that the owner’s ownership generally ceases. Kātyāyana states:
"According to the scriptures, possession (*bhukti*) is powerful when it is continuous and long-standing."
For that [possession] which was previously established should be understood as being even if interrupted; however,
as for that enjoyment which is continuous from the time of acquisition,
testimony regarding it generally proceeds once that acquisition has been reached.
In the period of memory (*smārta-kāla*), possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by a title (*sāgamā*).
However, in the period beyond memory (*asmārta*), due to the absence of a title, it is valid when it has been passed down through three generations in succession.

"Continuous" means uninterrupted; "long-standing" means it extends over the duration of time prescribed for Vyāsa and others. "Even if interrupted"—the meaning is that possession which was previously established by one's ancestors, such as the grandfather and so forth, should be understood as valid even if it has been interrupted.

He shows what is to be known by the word "ādāna" (acquisition): in both types of enjoyment previously mentioned—namely, that which is uninterrupted for only a short time and that which is interrupted—in both cases, when the *āgama* (title deed) which is their own basis is to be established, testimony (*sākṣya*) is generally the means of proof; this is the meaning.

Regarding the term *smārte*: it means "in a case suitable for recollection. *Kriyā* (action) refers to the means of proof (*pramāṇa*). *Āgama* refers to acquisition through purchase and so forth. Because of the absence of *āgama*—that is, because of the absence of a recollection of such acquisition—the meaning is as follows: possession (*bhukti*) accompanied by *āgama* is accepted as the means of proof regarding land during a period suitable for the recollection of *āgama*. However, during a period that has passed beyond the reach of recollection (*atipātini*), possession alone is the means of proof even in the absence of a recollection of *āgama*, and not merely upon the ascertainment of the absence of *āgama*; for in that latter case, ownership is denied by everyone.

Now, if possession (*bhukti*) accompanied by title (*āgama*) is the means of proof, then the qualification [of possession] is redundant. This is not so; for what is to be established here is: "This is now my own property. In this regard, the distinction is that title is the governing factor regarding the portion of ownership, whereas possession is the governing factor regarding its continued existence up to the present time.
Yājñavalkya (2.27): "But he who has made the title, when sued, must produce it."
Neither he nor his son [possesses the title]; in that case, possession is more weighty.

*Āgama* is the means of acquiring wealth, such as purchase and so forth. One who is diligent in that regard should clear up the title by proving it through documents and other evidence. However, for the son of that person, possession itself is the proof; the meaning is that he need not perform the purification of the title. Bṛhaspati says:
The acquirer shall establish possession and the title in court;
his son may establish only possession; his grandson and subsequent descendants may establish nothing at all.
"Acquirer" means the one who performed the acquisition.
Kātyāyana says:
For he by whom a property was taken up must restore it when sued;
even if there has been enjoyment for a long time, possession is not held to belong to him alone. [K 324]
The meaning is that even possession by an *arjaka* (one who has acquired the property) for a long time is not accepted as valid evidence without the manifestation of a legal title (*svāgama*).
When the acquirer is challenged, then the document or the witness is more authoritative;
for in the absence of a possessor, possession is indeed more weighty than those two in the case of a son.

The acquirer (arjaka) shall show documents and other evidence as proof of his own acquisition. In the absence of the acquirer, the meaning is that for his son, possession alone—supported by documents and so forth—is the proof.
[Verse 488] No force should be used in the enjoyment [of property] by the acquirer or by his son, in the case of cattle, women, men, and the like; such is the established law.

The word "beginning" (*ādipada*) refers to all things ending with moving property. Herein lies the settled rule: even for the acquirer, possession (*bhoga*) consisting of five factors is indeed valid evidence when there is an absence of documentary proof or witnesses; however, the [authoritative] statements [of the sages] must be understood as referring to the general case. Likewise, the prohibition regarding the validity of mere possession in the case of cattle and other such items is also to be interpreted as referring to the general case.
Yājñavalkya (4.89): "If one who is accused should die, his heir shall clear him [of the charge]."

In that case, possession (*bhukti*) established without a title (*āgama*) is not a cause [of ownership]. The meaning is as follows: if a person, while his property is being enjoyed by another, is accused and dies before a judicial determination has been made, his heir—such as a son or other successor—must recover that property for him by means of a title; in such a case, possession is not a valid means of proof, because it is counteracted by the prior accusation.

The moderns (*navyāḥ*) maintain that even when there is certainty regarding the absence of a title (*āgama*), possession for sixty years is a means of proof for ownership, based on the natural sense of such statements as, "that which has been enjoyed by another, [or] by one's father and three preceding ancestors," and so forth. This is not correct; for the author of the *Pārijāta*, while explaining that in the phrase "he enjoys without title" the singular number refers to the lineage (*santāna*), has utterly rejected this view by refusing to accept that ownership arises from mere possession even in the case of an object being enjoyed for many hundreds of years through a lineage consisting of a succession of fathers and sons.
Now, the exception to loss due to the possession of another is as follows:
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"Possession for three generations is established for others, there is no doubt;
however, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas. [B 7.43]
But property such as a house, field, or shop that has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner—

by a friend, a kinsman, or a relative— is not lost through such enjoyment. Likewise, property enjoyed by those who have performed marriages, by Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), or by the king’s ministers is not lost.
"Even after a very long time, that [desire] of theirs is not accomplished. The son-in-law is to be wedded.
— Manu.
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not lapse through mere possession.
— Bṛhaspati.

494. That which is recorded on a royal edict, even if enjoyed by another, is not lost once it has been enjoyed—[provided it was not taken] from those who are unattached, lazy, diseased, afflicted, children, frightened, or travelers. "Recorded on an edict" means inscribed upon a copper plate or similar medium.
Kātyāyana:

One should not assume ownership through mere possession in the case of women, the property of a king, the wealth of a *devara*, the property of a child or a *śrotriya*, or property inherited from a father in due order. [K 330]
496. There can be no enjoyment of women by any means whatsoever without a written document;
this is likewise held to be the case regarding the property of gods, Vedic scholars, kings, and minors.
— Manu.
497. "Things used through friendly consent are never lost; this applies to a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed as a beast of burden.
— Kātyāyana.
498. Property deposited with artisans for sale, as well as that which is pledged, entrusted for delivery, or borrowed;
"One who, out of delusion, forcibly seizes [property] should indeed be punished as a base person.
Here, *kraya* means that by which one buys; it is the price. — Yājñavalkya.

499. The king shall cause the person who misappropriates deposits and other such property to pay the wealth to the owner, and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or a fine according to his ability.
One who is unable to pay a fine equal to the value of the property should be punished according to his means.
And regarding these aforementioned immeasurable enjoyments, the intended meaning is established otherwise.
Now, concerning the relative strength and weakness of documentary evidence, witnesses, and possession,
Nārada says:

A document is always strong; however, living witnesses alone are authoritative. Through the lapse of time, possession becomes proof; such is the conclusion in the scriptures. Of these three types of visible evidence, in their respective order:

Each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative; possession is weightier than these. Regarding "each preceding one": the meaning is that a witness is more authoritative than possession, and a written document is more authoritative than that. The meaning is that possession endowed with five characteristics is weightier than these—namely, possession by witnesses and written documents of short duration. Bhavadeva reads, "possession is weightier than these two," which is indeed easy to understand.
However, this must be considered here: does this scriptural possession generate ownership for the possessor, or does it merely serve as proof of it?

In this regard, the following might be argued: First of all, this [enjoyment] is not a producer [of ownership], because, unlike the act of officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*), it is not heard in scripture as being a producer of ownership. Nor is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāpaka*). To explain: would it establish the ownership of the enjoyer by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), or by way of its own impossibility [otherwise]? It cannot be the first, because there is no apprehender of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between such enjoyment and ownership. Furthermore, if this were merely a means of cognizing pre-existing ownership, it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "that which has been enjoyed even unjustly," for one's own property is certainly not enjoyed unjustly. For this very reason, the second alternative is also not possible. Moreover, this "impossibility" does not apply to the wealth of women, kings, and so forth, since in those cases enjoyment is never a means of proof. Therefore, it must be stated thus: this aforementioned enjoyment implies the destruction of the previous owner’s ownership due to the former owner’s relinquishment of the object for the sake of the enjoyer. For it is not possible that he should not abandon it while still permitting such enjoyment of that thing. Furthermore, whatever is relinquished for the sake of someone is taken possession of by him and becomes his own; just as water and the like relinquished for the sake of all living beings [become theirs]. By this rule, this [object] also becomes the property of the enjoyer for that very reason. However, this is not the case with the wealth of women, kings, and others, because since a wife is not an object of [male] ownership and royal wealth is so extensive, the very act of relinquishment is impossible in those instances.

Regarding land and the like, possession for twenty years, and regarding cattle and the like, possession for ten years, serves as proof of the destruction of the previous owner’s ownership; this disparity in time is justified because land and such items yield great fruits and are the locus of immense value, and thus it is conceived that ownership is lost only after a long period. Likewise, since other types of property are not so, it is logical to conceive that ownership is lost even in a short period. Furthermore, the fact that the enjoyment of the possessor generates ownership specifically in the case of land and the like due to the disparity in time is also justified solely by the force of the scriptural statement, just as that very birth generates ownership over the father’s wealth for the son but not for the daughter.

On this point, the authors of the *Pradīpa* state: "For where a landowner, intending—'Since my deed has now been performed, there is no possibility here of obtaining the fruit; let another enjoy it for the time being, and later I shall take back this land together with its enjoyment from him'—consents [to the possession], there exists possession lasting twenty years, yet there is no relinquishment of his own property by the owner for that purpose. Because of such deviation, this [mere] possession is not a means of proof for the prior owner's relinquishment."

Nor should it be argued here that, because the former owner has not made a formal declaration of renunciation (*tyāga*), no ordeal (*divya*) need be administered; and that, consequently, if such an ordeal were to fail, there would be a determination of renunciation. Even so, since the prior possession established by previous enjoyment lacks the quality of being a time when renunciation is certain, it does not produce ownership in the enjoyer, and thus [the claim of the former owner] is futile. Furthermore, why would a conscious owner of land abandon it in vain? There is no visible motive (*dṛṣṭa*) here, as none exists; nor is there an invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*), due to the absence of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras. Moreover, renunciation may occur even through magnanimity, good character, compassion, and so forth; for it is possible that even while renouncing, he might still forgive [the enjoyer] on account of those very qualities. Nor is there a rule that "whatever is abandoned with a specific intent belongs to that person," because this is contradicted by cases where the intended recipient does not actually accept the gift.

Furthermore, the nature of the enjoyer’s ownership (*svatva*) arises either from renunciation (*tyāga*) or from knowledge (*jñāna*). It cannot be the former, because such a thing has never been observed. As for the second case, that knowledge would have to arise from the enjoyer’s own words or the like. And so, it would occur through the words of that owner preceded by his intention, thinking, "I have renounced this for his sake. Since this is simply an act of giving (*dāna*), there is no need to pursue the notion of indifference (*upekṣā*).

Nor can there be an inference of abandonment based solely on the aforementioned forbearance (*kṣamā*), because forbearance is possible even when there has been no abandonment, due to qualities such as good character (*sauśīlya*). It should not be argued that, in this way, there would likewise be no inference of the owner’s ownership (*svatva*) from the aforementioned forbearance, since the owner’s prior ownership might still exist there, and thus the forbearance could be accounted for otherwise by good character and so forth. For if forbearance were possible through good character and the like for as long as sixty years, then the rule stated in the Smṛti—that such enjoyment is a means of proving the owner’s ownership—would be violated. Therefore, such enjoyment is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the owner’s ownership. And whether that [ownership] arises from a prior transfer or from the former owner’s relinquishment of the object with the intent to benefit the enjoyer—on this point, we have no objection.
Yājñavalkya:
But he by whom the title-deed was executed, being accused, must produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more weighty.

When a doubt arises regarding the title of ownership (*āgama*), then only the person who brought forward the title (*ārjaka*) must prove that title. However, for his son, possession accompanied by that title (*sāgamā bhuktiḥ*) alone is the means of proof; this is the meaning.
But if the father, though previously accused, did not establish the purity of the title, then the son must indeed establish the purity of the title. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Likewise, when a litigant has died while the lawsuit was still pending..."
That matter must be cleared up by the son; possession shall not overturn it.
The meaning is that possession—mere possession—cannot overturn that legal dispute if it was established without a title (*āgama*).
Otherwise, there would be no proof [of ownership] through non-possession.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"Even possession has no strength where there is not even a slight amount of title" (YDh 2.27cd).

The meaning is that even when a title exists, ownership is not established for that duration of time due to the absence of possession. Here, the underlying principle is simply this: where something is given by someone to another person, ownership is not determined because of the lack of possession manifesting the recipient’s acceptance.

However, some explain it as follows: where the plaintiff and defendant proceed by the strength of their respective scriptures (*āgama*), and the priority between those two scriptures cannot be determined, the meaning is that the scripture of whichever party possesses possession (*bhukti*) is stronger, not that of the other.
Nārada [states]: "Even when a written document exists, and even while witnesses are alive..."
In particular, that which is not enjoyed, such as immovable property and the like, does not remain secure.
When one neglects out of delusion objects being enjoyed by others,
even while he is alive and present, their enjoyment brings those objects under the control of the other.

That [property] is not stable; that is to say, it does not possess a means of proof establishing ownership that persists for a long period of time. The meaning is this: if one, out of delusion, neglects objects being enjoyed by another, no other wealth shall be recoverable from the side of that enjoyer on account of the connection with such enjoyment, precisely because of his own negligence.
On this very point, Yājñavalkya says:
"For land, there is loss after twenty years for one who sees [the enjoyment] but does not speak."
"Regarding property being enjoyed by another, the period is ten years. Vyāsa says:
"Just as a cow perishes through neglect when left without a keeper,"
Land enjoyed by others while one looks on is lost over time.
(Vy 1.76) If land has been enjoyed here by others for twenty years, even while a capable king is present, that possession is not established for him. (Vy 1.77)
Nārada:
However, through actual enjoyment, ownership is lost after twenty years; even deposits and the like are forfeited, except for the property of a woman or a king.
"Twelve years" means twenty years. Regarding the phrase "even mortgages and so forth," this should not be understood as being like the injunction "it is better that you eat poison.
[N 1.81]: "A mortgage, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar are not extinguished by mere enjoyment."
By such words of Nārada, the wearing out of a pledge through enjoyment is prohibited. Manu [says]:
"Both a pledge and a deposit do not suffer by the lapse of time."

Those two, having remained for a long time, shall become forfeitable. [M 8.145] *Ādhi* means a pledge; *upanidhi* refers to fields or other property handed over out of friendship for the purpose of enjoyment. They do not deserve the lapse of time; the meaning is that they must necessarily be released at the time of redemption. The reason for this is stated as "forfeitable," and so forth. For those two, having remained for a long time, would become forfeitable to the enjoyer alone—the sense being that the enjoyer might perhaps seize them. Bṛhaspati says:
513. If property is delivered in the presence of others by heirs or other persons to one who subsequently enjoys it, another person does not deserve to recover that [property].
514. He who, seeing another giving away land, does not prevent it—[is liable for the loss].
Even with a document, the owner shall not recover that [property] again.
Likewise:
"Non-enjoyment of land and the failure to produce a document at the proper time..."
And the failure to remind witnesses of their duties leads to the ruin of one's own interests.
Therefore, one must diligently maintain the integrity of the means of proof;
by that, both immovable and movable matters are successfully resolved.
And thus, the essential point is that statements regarding loss are intended solely for the preservation of the means of proof.
Now follows the determination of interrupted enjoyment.
On this matter, Bṛhaspati says:

517. Where possession has been interrupted or where there is doubt regarding a house or field, one should establish that matter by means of a written document, those who know of the possession, or witnesses.
518. [The document should record] the name, the boundaries, the title of acquisition, the number, the direction and location, and the time.

And those who know of the cause for the interruption of their enjoyment are the witnesses in this matter. Furthermore, those neighboring landowners born from that [original grant] who reside in other regions are designated as the primary (maula) witnesses; they should be questioned in the determination of the legal case.

520. This has been declared regarding immovable property for the purpose of establishing gain and enjoyment. But in a dispute lacking proof, divine means of proof (*daivikī kriyā*) are to be prescribed.

"Disputed" means the doubt regarding the name of a field or similar property. "Boundary" (*āghāṭa*) refers to the limit. "Title" (*āgama*) is the cause of ownership. "Number" pertains to the land itself. "Directional portion" (*digbhāga*) also pertains to that same land. "Time" is the time of acquisition. "In a dispute lacking proof" means in a dispute where the perceived proof is lacking.
Thus ends the section on possession (*bhukti*). Now, regarding title (*yukti*),
Bṛhaspati says:
522. In a case where no witnesses are present or when it has been wrongly decided, he should question subsequent witnesses, or he should administer oaths, or he should employ a stratagem (*upadhā*).
A stratagem (*upadhā*) is a clever device.
Nārada: 523. Where, due to negligence, there is neither a document nor witnesses for a creditor, and the plaintiff denies the claim, the threefold procedure prescribed therein shall apply. [N 1.235]

524. An accusation at the proper time, as well as a fragment of reasoning, and thirdly, an oath—by these means one should resolve the matter in due order. 525. Even when being repeatedly accused, if he should reject those words...

He may cause the other to pay the debt three, four, or five times, or even more than that. *Codanā* is the repeated urging, at the appropriate time, saying, "Give me my own wealth. Thus says Kātyāyana.
When a matter is being announced by a petitioner and is not obstructed,
or when one remains silent at the time of the gift, that matter is deemed approved. Where one does not cause an obstruction while accompanied by the petitioner himself, [that too is approval].
If he does not pay after being told three, four, or five times, or thereafter, he becomes a debtor.
The king should cause the owner to make the *vipra* pay what was declared as the debt;
other than that, he should cause him to pay who did not fail when told once.

When a creditor, the master, has requested, saying "Give me my wealth," he should cause a Brahmin who has not resisted [the demand] to pay it gradually; however, the meaning is that for one who is not a Brahmin, [he may do so] even by such means as force. Others say the meaning is: a Brahmin must be made to pay wealth that was requested more than once and not resisted, whereas one who is not a Brahmin must be made to pay even wealth requested only once, provided it was not resisted. Nārada says:
"But when there is resistance to the demand, one should pursue him through subtle applications of reasoning."
By means of place, time, object, relation, measure, action, and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: when a debtor denies the claim, saying "I do not owe anything," then a determination must be made through arguments known by another name as inference (*anumāna*). For example: if, in a certain place, at a certain time, and for a certain purpose or motive, a creditor has brought a charge against a debtor for the taking of a loan, yet it is impossible that he took such a loan under those circumstances of place and so forth for that purpose, then the determination is made through reasoning (*yukti*). Likewise, even in the case of one who has no possibility of owing even a hundred, if he should say, "A thousand was taken from me by him," there too the determination is made through the reasoning of quantity (*parimāṇa-yukti*). Similarly, where the actions of the debtor and so forth are perceived as being in the form of small increments paid every month, there too it is determined through reasoning.
Now, an oath shall be described from this point.
Thus, by means of the proof of a single part, Nārada has stated that the entire subject matter of the dispute must be paid:
"By one who is accused on multiple counts but denies the whole matter... (NSm 1.530).
"It is also appropriate to give even that which has been partially cultivated. Thus [it is said]. [N?]

In a case where several items, such as gold, silver, and so forth, have been taken together in a single vessel, the scope of that plea is not the entire collection of items on the grounds of a conceptualization (*vibhāvanā*) regarding the taking of only one substance; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the existence of the other substances when they have not been conceptually distinguished. Indeed, their establishment cannot result from the mere word of the plaintiff, since the possibility of falsehood also exists. Nor can the plaintiff’s presence therein at that time be made known by the opponent through another means of proof, such as witnesses; for if that were so, it would follow that the statement [of the plea] would become useless, since the matter could be decided by that other means alone. Rather, its scope is that which is pervaded by the taking of the other items whenever there is a taking of one. Or else, its scope is that case where the litigant accepts: "If you can even demonstrate one among those items thus implicated, then the whole must be given by me. This is the scope of that plea.
Nārada: 531. Other six types of disputes are declared to be those where there is no reliance on witnesses;
the wise say that for these, the very characteristics [of the case] constitute the basis for witness-status.

One with a torch in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer; and one seized by the hair is an adulterer caught in the act. One with a spade in hand is to be recognized as a destroyer of embankments when found nearby.
Likewise, a forest-cutter with an axe in his hand is well known;
a man who commits physical assault is to be recognized by these visible marks.
For in cases of assault, these are matters to be determined even without witnesses; thus there must be an investigation into the violence.

"In the state of being a witness" means in the position of a witness. Their status as witnesses is due to their invariable concomitance with the visible signs, such as blood, wounds, swords, and so forth. Regarding "assault," that is, verbal assault, Kātyāyana says:
"Giving, intimidation, sowing dissension, and the act of association."
And the removal of wealth—these indeed are the causes that bring about dissipation.

"Giving" refers to the giving of bribes. "Sowing discord through instigation" refers to altering a characteristic mark by which something is recognized. "The act of association" refers to generating excessive greed for another object. Śaṅkha says:

536, 537. One who seizes another by the hair is an adulterer; one with a torch in hand is an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer; and one with plunder in hand is a thief. In the case of an insult, the fine is eight hundred [paṇas], or according to the specific nature of the act. In the case of visible bloodshed or a manifest blow, there are no witnesses; and when the evidence is clearly manifested, the fine is eight hundred. Regarding "insult" (*kṣepa*), this refers to the denial of a blow established by the aforementioned signs. The remainder of the sentence is that the punishment is a fine of eight hundred *paṇas*.

Furthermore, these methods of reasoning, being of the nature of inference based on grounds that are difficult to ascertain and not otherwise established, are not common to all; rather, they rest solely upon the judgment of those who are extremely skilled. And this very [process] is also called "determination through perception. Now, concerning the divine ordeals (*divya*):
regarding this, Nārada says:
Even when the logical arguments are insufficient, one should distress the defendant with oaths,

taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength of the parties, by means of fire, water, good deeds, and so forth. The balance, fire, water, poison, and fifthly, the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals.

These divine methods have been declared by the great-souled ones for the sake of purification. They were proclaimed here by Nārada for the purpose of examining those who are accused in doubtful cases, so that there may be purification regarding truth and falsehood.

*Ardayet* means "he should afflict" or "torment. Regarding *agni*: throwing one's hand into fire or water with the thought, "Fire will not attend to me" or "Water will carry me away," constitutes [the test]. An oath consists of such things as thinking, "My merit (*sukṛta*) will perish. Now, it will be stated that fire and the like are to be understood here as *divya* (ordeals), because they are distinct from oaths.
But surely other *divya* ordeals have also been mentioned by Bṛhaspati? As he says:
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
the sixth is said to be rice-grains, and the seventh is the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka).
The eighth is called the plowshare, and the ninth shall be that which arises from Dharma.
"All these divine [sciences] were taught by the Self-Existent One. Likewise:
"I shall state them in brief for the sake of purifying doubtful meanings."
These [gifts], joined with respect to place, time, purpose, and number, in due order,
should be given according to the nature of the offense and with the intention of communicating what is right or wrong, following the very procedure prescribed in the scriptures and not otherwise.

The "drinking from the vessel" (*kośapāna*)—the drinking of water from a vessel containing a trident and other objects measured by three of one's own handfuls—is indeed true; however, it was specifically prescribed by Yājñavalkya. As he says:
"Tula (the balance), fire, water, and poison are the ordeals for the sake of purification here;
these are used in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]. [YDh 2.95]

And thus, it is restricted that these [ordeals] are to be used only in cases of great accusation (*mahābhiyoga*) and not elsewhere; however, it is not the case that these alone are the divine ordeals (*divya*). Even in a great accusation, they are not employed everywhere, but only when the accuser is "staked on his head" (*śīrṣakastha*). "Head" (*śīrṣa*) means the head; and in this context, it refers to the accuser’s winning side or his acceptance of the penalty. 546. Held upon a scale by experts in weighing, the accused, having been made equal to the counterweight and having had a written record prepared, is placed upon the balance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.100)
547. O Balance, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt. 548.
If this man is a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward.
If he is pure, he should consecrate the balance with the words, "Lead me upward. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.102) 549. If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he is purified; of this there is no doubt.
If he remains equal or decreases in weight, the man shall not be considered pure. (Nārada Smṛti 1.283)
The Grandfather said:
"The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and the two supports should likewise be made so; the distance between them should be two cubits, or even two and a half. [Pi 87]
But in the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
"You alone, O balance-beam, know those things which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal proceeding, is being weighed upon you."
Therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt by means of dharma.
(Vi 10.11cd) Those worlds that are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, those worlds for one who gives false testimony,
and those worlds for a weigher of scales who holds the balance falsely— (Vi 10.9)
Vyāsa says: One who moves downward is not pure; one who moves upward is always pure. Even one who is stationary is not pure. This is declared to be purity. [Vy 2.17]

555. "In the case of the breaking of the frame, the snapping of the balance-beam, or likewise of the *dhaṭa* and *karkaṭa*, as well as the cutting of the rope or the failure of the axle, one should administer the ordeal again and again. Regarding the word "balance" (*tulā*): the meaning of the verse is that the accused person, having fasted and so forth, is weighed on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). On the following morning, after he has been consecrated with mantras, he is to be weighed again; if he rises upward, then he is the victor, but if not, he is defeated. This is the essential point.
Having observed that his two hands have rubbed the grains of rice,

he should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread. Likewise, having provided *śamī* wood, unhusked grain, and *dūrvā* grass, he should arrange them upon the leaves.
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, declare the truth regarding merits and sins for me, as I hold this [vow] in my hand.
When he has spoken thus, [the judge shall take] an iron [ball] weighing fifty palas, which is smooth...
He should place a ball of fire-colored clay upon both hands.
Taking it, he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles;
each circle should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths in width, with an equal interval between them.

561. One who has released the fire, whose rice-grains have been crushed, and who remains unburned shall attain purification; if the ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, he shall take it up again. 562.
The ball, glowing like fire, with sparks and well-guarded...
Having further caused a [weight] of fifty palas to be made, the pure twice-born man,
placing truth before him, should speak to the one undergoing the third heating:
"Listen to this law of Manu, presided over by the world-protectors."
564. O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
you alone, O Agni, know those things which human beings do not know. 565. This man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Therefore, the Grandfather ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
"One should not go in haste; rather, being composed, one should go very slowly. [Vi 11.12 = Pi 127]
One should not step over the *maṇḍala*, nor should one place a foot within it.
Having gone to the eighth *maṇḍala*, the wise man should set down [the foot] on the ninth.
— Yājñavalkya.

If the accused stumbles or burns something other than the designated spot, the gods do not consider him burnt; one should have him burn it once more. Then, being purified, he should cast either rice grains or barley seeds into those two fires.
570. "But if they have been rubbed with both hands without distinction, one should declare his purification at the end of the day, provided there has been no change [in his condition].
— Viṣṇu.
One whose hands have been burnt in any place should be declared impure;
but that man who is not burnt at all shall be pure. [Vi 11.8]

Having performed the preliminary rites such as fasting and consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day, the accused stands in the first mandala on the following day. Having examined his hands, he places upon them two seven-leaved *aśvattha* leaves wrapped with thread, smeared with barley and *dūrvā* grass, and upon which iron [weights] have been placed. Then, having stepped through the six mandalas in succession, he stands in the eighth and casts the iron [weight] in the ninth. "In case of doubt regarding whether he has crossed the mandalas or not, he should take it back again"—this is the collective meaning.
"O Varuṇa, protect me by truth," thus chanting the *Kam* [hymn].
Standing in water reaching up to his navel, he should enter the water after grasping his thigh.

[Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.108] If another swift man, having released an arrow at that same moment, should see him with his limbs submerged when the arrow has passed, he would obtain the reward for piercing the target. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.109]
574. Otherwise, it would not be pure, because even a single factor might be seen;
whether by remaining in place or by going elsewhere, one should first establish [the deity] therein with the words, "By truth."
575. O Water, you move within all beings like a witness;
you alone know those waters which human beings do not know.
576. This man, accused in a legal dispute, is now immersed in you.
Therefore, he ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma. Likewise:
"Then another man of similar character, taking up a middle-sized arrow..."
He should return with speed from where that man was held;
but when the arrow-retriever, having arrived, does not see him properly within the water,
then one should declare him purified.
579. When the arrow has been drawn out and his limbs have sunk, he shall attain purity.
Kātyāyana states: 580. Only the head should be visible, neither the ears nor the nose.
One should also declare him pure who, upon entering the waters,
surfaces again; provided that the man is seen by a living being while floating,
he should dive in once more, his identity confirmed by the marks on his limbs.

Standing in water that reaches up to his navel, the accused person should submerge his thighs while holding onto it. At that very moment, one strong man should shoot an arrow, and another strong man should retrieve it. If he has submerged himself entirely within that interval, or even with only a single limb, and emerges back to the surface or returns to his former position, then he is not defeated; otherwise, he is.
582 "O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness.
Protect us from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.110]
Having spoken thus, he should consume the Śārṅga poison born of the snowy mountains.
If it is digested by him without causing disease, one should declare him pure.
Regarding the word "thou" (*tvam*): the meaning is that if the poison named Śārṅga, having been consumed according to the prescribed rule, produces no adverse effect, then the accused is victorious.
Regarding the drinking from the vessel (*kośapāna*), the passage beginning with "the gods" and so forth is easy to understand:
"Having worshipped fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having caused [the accused] to hear [the oath], one should then make him drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of that water. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.112]
585. He for whom no terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, occurs until the fourteenth day, shall be proven innocent; of this there is no doubt. Thus said Pitāmaha.
One should avoid divine ordeals that are devoid of the head and so forth;
however, the four beginning with the *dhaṭa* (balance) and the *kośa* (oath) are traditionally held to be without heads.
Likewise—

587. No one should compel the plaintiff to undergo an ordeal; those expert in ordeals should administer the ordeal only to the defendant. Regarding this as well, Nārada states that there is no need to consider the king’s command.
588. When a litigant has arrived who is ready to stake his very life, the administration of ordeals is prescribed;
otherwise, there is the royal decree.
— Yājñavalkya.
589. Or, by mutual consent, one party may perform the ordeal while the other undergoes the penalty;
or even without the penalty, one may perform it in cases of treason against the king or mortal sin.

By mutual agreement between the accuser and the accused, the accuser alone may perform it, because the nature of the means of proof known as "divine ordeal" applies regardless of whether the charge is true or false.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa (590): "In cases of false accusation regarding another's wife, in theft, in the unauthorized entry into a fire-sanctuary,
and in those censured for mortal sins (mahāpātaka), there shall be an ordeal under royal decree."
When a disagreement arises in a dispute and a wager has been established,
the king shall administer the ordeal right there, beginning with the one whose head was first mentioned.
592. In cases of approaching another's wife where there are many disputants, the ordeal shall be one involving decapitation for the purpose of self-purification.

In the case of a dispute regarding adultery or false accusations concerning another's wife; in legal disputes such as those involving debts; and "adultery with another's wife" is also an elliptical expression that includes theft and other such acts.
Viṣṇu states: "In cases of treason against the king and in violent crimes, [the ordeal may be performed] even without the application of the head. [Vi 9.22]
The Grandfather said:
For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,
and for those intent on proving their own purity, the ordeal should be administered with the exception of the "head" ordeal.
Nārada:
"And one should cause divine ordeals to be administered to the king's servants.
Bṛhaspati: [595]
"Witnesses may fall into discord due to affection, anger, or greed; however, no such discord ever arises regarding a divine ordeal prescribed by rule. Thus spoke Pitāmaha.
The king, or his authorized official, shall cause the ordeal to be administered directly to learned Brāhmaṇas and likewise to the subjects. (Viṣṇu and Kātyāyana).
Having summoned one who has fasted and bathed with his clothes on at sunrise,

the judge should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and the Brahmins. On the previous day, having fasted and bathed with his clothes on, the person undergoing the ordeal should have all the divine tests administered by the judge at sunrise, in the presence of the king, the members of the court, and the Brahmins.
The Grandfather said:
To one who has fasted for three nights, or even for one night, who is pure and wears wet garments, divine gifts should always be given. [Pi 53]
And this option of fasting for three nights or one night is established according to one's capacity and according to whether the charge is grave or minor. Likewise:
"The judge shall conduct all judicial proceedings involving ordeals."
Just as the Adhvaryu priest observes a fast during the sacrificial rites by the king’s command,
so too does this judge observe a fast when he is entitled to perform divine worship as part of the ordeal.
Although it is stated here without qualification that "at sunrise," nevertheless, according to the practice of the learned, Sunday is observed.
Likewise:
"The examination by fire should take place in the forenoon, and the balance should be used in the forenoon;
however, water should be administered at midday for one who desires the true nature of Dharma. [Pi 45]
602. However, the purification by means of the *kośa* (sacred water) is prescribed for the forenoon of the day;
whereas poison should be administered at night during the last watch, when it is very cool.
For those [ordeals] such as rice (*taṇḍula*) for which no specific time has been mentioned, the administration occurs only in the forenoon.
"The administration of all ordeals is proclaimed to take place in the forenoon," according to the *Nārada-smṛti*.
Kātyāyana states the appropriate location for these ordeals:

604. For men who have been accused in the place of Indra, for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), and for those who have engaged in treason against the king, one should employ the ordeal at the royal gate. 605.
For those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), the divine ordeal should be administered at a crossroads.
Therefore, the wise know that in other matters as well, the assembly hall is the place for deliberation;
it is Indra’s place, the place of Indra’s banner,
and the abode of Bṛhaspati.
606. The ordeal must be administered according to the prescribed rules by those expert in ordeals;
however, one administered contrary to the rules is not capable of proving the matter to be established.
607. Those administered at an improper place or time, or those performed outside the presence of the plaintiff, are likewise invalid.

"In this world, they always commit such transgression; of this there is no doubt. [B 8.16] This refers to one who acts without an accuser, even though an external challenger has been made. And this is the general rule, for those intent on self-purification perform the divine ordeals even without an accuser. Katyayana says:
Furthermore, one should establish the matter to be proven when there is a contradiction in the proof;
for even though the divine ordeals have been administered as prescribed,
the king should avoid them if they are performed by fools, the greedy, or the wicked, and indeed they must be administered again.
The meaning is that if, for some reason, there remains a doubt regarding the validity of the previous ordeal, the ordeal must be administered again.
Now, Pitāmaha states the specific times and procedures for each particular type of ordeal:
"Whatever time has been prescribed for whichever [ordeal], and whatever procedure for whichever, in whatever manner..."
I shall explain that in its true nature, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the disputants:
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these are the common months, which are not adverse to the celestial beings.
The water-jar is said to be suitable for all seasons; however, one should avoid it when the wind is blowing. Fire is proclaimed to be beneficial during the cold, winter, and rainy seasons;
water during the autumn and summer; and poison during the late winter and early spring.
Nārada: 613. There shall be no purification by water during the cold season, nor purification by fire during the heat;
the king should not administer poison in the rainy season, nor a balance scale in a high wind.
Here, by the word "cold" (śīta), the winter, the dewy season, and the rainy season are included; by the word "hot" (uṣṇa), the autumn and the summer are included. According to Jyotiṣa:
"When Jupiter is situated in Leo or Capricorn, or when Venus has set..."
In an intercalary month, those who desire victory should not perform an examination.
When the sun is impure, when Jupiter has set, and again when Venus has set,
as well as when the sun is in conjunction with the moon, examination is not recommended by the wise.
616. On the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, there should be neither penance nor examination;
nor should the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for an examination take place on a Saturday or a Tuesday.
Now, regarding the specific distinctions based on caste, Nārada states:
"The balance should be given to a Brāhmaṇa; fire to a Kṣatriya;
water should be given to a Vaiśya; and poison alone to a Śūdra. (NSm 1.334cd–335ab)

The wise have declared that the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) is common to all, while for a Brāhmaṇa, all ordeals are prescribed except for poison; or rather, the ordeal by scales (*tulā*) is ordained for everyone.
— Kātyāyana.
620. One should administer the fire ordeal to a Kṣatriya, the balance ordeal to a Brāhmaṇa, and water to a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any divine ordeal for all castes, except the poison ordeal, for the most excellent of the twice-born.
— Yājñavalkya.
