621. For women, children, the elderly, the afflicted, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by the balance; for a Śūdra, by fire or water; or seven grains of poison may be used.
— Kātyāyana.
622. One should cause the twice-born to employ cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers in the same manner as Śūdras;
so says Nārada.

623. One should always examine eunuchs, the sick, those lacking in strength, men afflicted by intense suffering, as well as children, the elderly, and the infirm, regarding their fitness for the ordeal by balance (*dhaṭa*). 624.
For the afflicted, purification by water is not permitted; nor is poison suitable for those suffering from bilious diseases.

The fire-ritual is not prescribed for those afflicted with leprosy, blindness, deformed nails, and the like. Those learned in the Dharmaśāstras should not cause women, children, the sick, the elderly, or men who are weak to enter the water for immersion.
One should not cause those who are lacking in vigor, afflicted by disease, or distressed to be submerged in water;
for they are considered to have very little life-force and would die instantly while being submerged.
Even if these individuals have arrived for the purpose of a daring act, one must never submerge them in water.
Nor should one cause fire to be carried away, nor should one purify it by means of a ladle. Kātyāyana says:
Fire is not [to be used] for metal-workers, nor water for those who subsist on water.
One who knows the application of mantras and yoga should never administer poison.
One should always avoid the divine ordeal for men afflicted by diseases.
One should not employ the rice-ordeal for those observing vows or for those suffering from mouth diseases.
To one who observes a vow—that is, one observing the vow of not eating rice—[one should give].
Viṣṇu [states]: 631–633. Fire should not be given to those suffering from leprosy, to the incapable, or to those who work with iron. This applies during the autumn and summer seasons.

634–635. Poison should not be administered to lepers, those afflicted with bile disorders, or Brāhmaṇas; nor during the rainy season. 636. Water should not be administered to those suffering from phlegmatic diseases, the timid, those with asthma or coughing fits, or those who subsist on water.
637–638. Nor during the winter and early spring seasons. The ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) should not be given to atheists, nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence.
The Grandfather said:
639. “And likewise for those addicted to drinking liquor and women, as well as for gamblers.”
The treasury should not be given away by the wise to those who follow the conduct of nihilists. Kātyāyana says:
But when there is no conflict with place and time, one should arrange it as is appropriate.
One may have another perform the ordeal; this is the rule in the case of the opposite circumstance.

"By another" means by a representative. "He may have it performed" means he should cause it to be done. "In the opposite circumstance" refers to the incapacity of the person formally charged with the case.
Nārada says:
641. "The ordeal shall not be administered to those who observe vows, those who are emaciated or afflicted, those who are diseased, ascetics, and women, if Dharma is to be regarded.
— Kātyāyana.
For those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king;

for those burdened with the great sins (mahāpātaka); especially for atheists; for those wearing the marks of religious orders (liṅgin); for women; and for those who know the practice of mantras and yogic rites— [K 427] 643.
In these very cases of accusation involving those born of mixed castes who persist in sinful practices,
a king devoted to dharma should not, with any effort, prescribe an ordeal for such contemptible matters.
645. By these very means, the ordeal is appropriate for virtuous persons who are accused;
but where virtuous persons do not accept it, there the matter should be proven by their own kinsmen.
646. [This applies] especially in cases involving those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātaka) and those who are atheists (nāstika).

Bhṛgu says that the divine ordeals must not be administered to those who are habitually engaged in sinful acts. (K 431) 647 Those in whom the performance of divine ordeals has been strictly prohibited due to their sins—these cases should be investigated by virtuous men; the king must not abandon an accused person on that basis alone. (K 432)
Regarding the specific rule for those accused of *avaṣṭambha* (defiance), the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) says:
"For those accused of *avaṣṭambha*, one should cause ordeals such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) to be administered;
however, in cases of suspicion, one should employ these two: rice (*taṇḍula*) and the oath (*kośa*). [Pi 36]
In this context, "avaṣṭambha" means certainty. Likewise:
"For those accused on suspicion of theft, the ordeal of the heated gold coin (taptamāṣa) is prescribed. [Pi 169cd]

Kātyāyana: In cases involving suspicion, the establishment of trust, or a dispute among heirs, and whenever one is acting as the performer of a collective undertaking, the judge should always cause the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) to be administered.
Regarding the agency in a collection of actions— that is, the performance of a single action by acting together—
Pitāmaha states: "In matters of trust, in all types of suspicion, and likewise in the business of making peace."
Among these, a treasury should always be provided for the sake of the purification of the mind.
In this regard, there is a specific divine distinction determined by the number of substances;
concerning that, Viṣṇu says:

652–654. Now, the performance of the ordeal (*samayakriyā*). In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, it may be administered at will. In cases of deposits, debts, and theft, it depends on the value of the object. An ordeal is called *samaya*. In cases such as treason against the king, "at will" means that the ordeal is to be administered according to the king's desire. This is the meaning.
In the context of the phrase "divine procedure," Bṛhaspati states:

"In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual disagreement, a document endowed with the details of the property's value should be given, taking into account the status of the individuals involved. [B 8.7]
Kātyāyana:
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should establish proof;
in cases of theft and violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.

One should calculate [the value] and know the number of items that have been concealed. Regarding the phrase "even when small": the meaning is that even in the case of a debt or the like that is so small as to preclude the use of an ordeal—such as in cases of theft or violence—even for wealth of that same small amount, an ordeal may be employed. Bṛhaspati says:
"The number [of grains] has been declared by Manu to be based on a ray of light, a particle of dust, and a root."

In matters of divine ordeal, that [fine] should be applied up to one *kārṣāpaṇa* in civil disputes (*vinaya*). Poison is to be used when a thousand [coins] have been stolen; fire when three-quarters of a thousand; water when two-thirds of a thousand have been stolen; and the balance is always to be employed for half of a thousand.
659. When the charge involves four hundred [paṇas], the heated *māṣaka* coin must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains are to be given, and for half of that (one hundred and fifty), the ordeal by sacred water (*kośa*).
660. When one hundred has been stolen or denied, the purification by sacred law (*dharmaśodhana*) must be administered.
The members of the court shall inflict the punishment of licking a red-hot plowshare upon a cow-thief.
This scale of punishment prescribed by the investigators is for the lowest class; it is recorded as being double for the middle class, and fourfold for the highest class.
*Raśmirajomūlā* – 662: When the sun has passed through a lattice, that subtle particle of dust which is seen is declared to be the first of all measurements, the *trasareṇu*. [M 8.132]

And so forth. The subsequent numbers are also according to this sequence. Regarding punishment (*daṇḍa*) in the Vinaya: for those who are lowly by birth, quality, or action; likewise for those who are middling and those who are superior.
Yājñavalkya (6.63): One should not take [a case] involving more than a thousand [paṇas], nor poison, nor a balance.

In matters concerning the king, in cases of accusation, and always when they are pure, they shall bear [the penalty]. [The meaning of "not from a thousand" is "less than a thousand *paṇas*. "In matters concerning the king" means in acts of treason against the king or regarding the king's property. "In cases of accusation" means in charges of heinous crimes (*pātaka*). "Always" means even without the previously mentioned amounts. "Pure" means through bathing and other such purifications. However, they say that these mentions of "a thousand" and so forth refer specifically to the subjects of theft and violence (*sāhasa*).

Viṣṇu (664, 665): For all types of objects, one should determine the value in gold. In that regard, for a debt of one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding *dūrvā* grass; for two *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding sesame seeds; for three *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding silver.

If the value is four *kṛṣṇalas*, the ordeal shall be the balance (*kanaka-kara*). If it is five *kṛṣṇalas*, it shall be the earth drawn from a furrow (*sītoddhṛta-mahī-kara*). For a Śūdra, when the value is half a *suvarṇa*, the treasury (*kośa*) must be administered. Beyond that, one of the ordeals—the balance, fire, water, or poison—should be applied according to the circumstances. For a Vaiśya, when the value is double [that], the conventional procedure (*samaya-kriyā*) as prescribed shall apply; for a value triple [that], [the same applies].

674, 675. [This applies] to a Kṣatriya; for a Brāhmaṇa, it is fourfold. One should not make a Brāhmaṇa pay a fine. 676, 677. Except in the case of an agreement made for the sake of future time. And in place of a fine, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by the earth produced from a furrow. Even in a matter of small value, one who has been previously seen to be guilty [should be so sworn].
One should cause only one of the divine ordeals to be performed; for that conduct is well known among the virtuous, and it is not required in a matter of great importance.

In this context, the term *kanaka* refers to gold as a measure of weight. Regarding that gold: having placed *dūrvā* grass and other items in order upon his hand, an oath must be taken by a *śūdra*. "Half a *suvarṇa*" means half a *kanaka*. When the value of the object is half a *suvarṇa*, a *śūdra* must undergo the ordeal of drinking from the *kośa* (sacred water). For twice that amount, a *vaiśya* may do so; for three times that, a *kṣatriya*; and for four times that, a *brāhmaṇa* must perform those same oaths. Regarding the wealth corresponding to the *śūdra’s* *kośa* ordeal, for amounts double or triple that, the *vaiśya* and *kṣatriya* should likewise undergo the *kośa* ordeal, but the *brāhmaṇa* should not be made to undergo the *kośa*. However, "elsewhere" (*anyatra*)—that is, in a case where an agreement has been made such as "we shall act together in this manner"—the *brāhmaṇa* may indeed be made to undergo the *kośa*. *Sītā* is the furrow-mark of a plough. "According to what is appropriate" (*yathārham*) means: even for a small matter in cases of theft or violence, but in cases of debt and the like, when the accusation involves hundreds of *suvarṇas* or more.
Kātyāyana:
Having ascertained the value of all the goods involved, one should determine the amount of gold;
then, one should employ the ordeal according to the prescribed measure of that gold. [K 417]

681. At ninety-seven [palas], poison is administered; at ninety-three, the fire-ordeal is seen there; at sixty-seven, the water-ordeal; and at fifty, the balance-ordeal is prescribed. 682. Or the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) may be used at forty-five, fifty, or seventy.
Half of that amount should be given in rice, and half of that again in a *taptamāṣaka*.

This means [the ordeal applies] when the sum is one hundred *suvarṇas*. When the wealth is three-quarters less—that is, when the sum is one hundred *suvarṇas* minus one-third—it is half of that, meaning half of fifty. Regarding "in ten, five, or seven": the meaning is that the *kośapāna* (drinking from the vessel) ordeal should be administered when the sum is a tenth, a fifth, or a seventh part of one hundred.
And in this context, a small quantity refers to a case involving a low-ranking person.
Vṛddha-Manu:
"Having ascertained the quantity of gold, poison is prescribed for a loss of one hundred;
but for a loss of eighty, one should indeed administer fire."
685. If sixty [coins] are lost, water should be known as the ordeal; for forty, the balance;
or, according to Bṛhaspati, for the loss of thirty or ten, the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna).
686. Or, if five or half of that are lost, rice grains (taṇḍula) [should be used].

"Or upon the destruction of thirty or ten" means: upon the destruction of thirty or the destruction of ten. "Or upon the destruction of half of five" means: upon the destruction of half of five or half of that [half], there is the ordeal of drinking from the vessel (*kośapāna*).

These statements, however, concern subjects such as debts and superior matters; therefore, there is no contradiction with Yājñavalkya and others. As for the subject matter of ordeals (*divya*), they are not elaborated here for fear of excessive length.
Now, regarding oaths:
on this matter, Manu says:
"One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons."
A Vaiśya with cattle, seed, and gold; a Śūdra with all types of heinous crimes.
Furthermore, one should have him touch the heads of his son and wife individually.

One should cause [the person] to swear by truth, making him declare: "If this was done by me, then may I become a partaker of the sin arising from the transgression of truth. Regarding the phrase "by vehicles and weapons," the meaning is that one should likewise make him declare: "If this was done by me, then may these vehicles or weapons become useless to me. The same applies elsewhere. Halāyudha, however, has explained: "A Brāhmaṇa must say 'Truth'; a Kṣatriya must touch a vehicle or a weapon; a Vaiśya must touch any one of cow, seed, or gold; and a Śūdra must perform all of these. Furthermore, he explained that the word *pātaka* (sin) here is a qualification of the aforementioned oaths, because those [oaths], when taken in vain, are the cause of sin.
Bṛhaspati: Truth is the vehicle and the weapon; cows, seed-corn, and gold;
the feet of the gods and Brahmins; and the heads of one’s sons and wife.

690. "These oaths have been declared by Manu for minor matters; however, in cases of violence (*sāhasa*) and false accusation (*abhiśāpa*), ordeals (*divya*) are the means of purification. Since these oaths are presented here as distinct from ordeals and are not included among the *ghaṭa* (balance) and other such tests, they do not possess the nature of an ordeal. Consequently, it should be understood that the ritual requirements of ordeals—such as fasting, wearing wet clothes, and so forth—do not apply; rather, there is merely the requirement of bathing and sipping water for the sake of purity.
Śaṅkha:
691. He should cause the performance of the giving of *iṣṭāpūrta* and other oaths.
Manu: [ŚL 265]
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking false oaths, he perishes both in this world and after death.
[M 8.111] In matters concerning women, marriages, cattle, food, and likewise fuel—

"And there is no sin in taking an oath for the sake of assisting a Brāhmaṇa" (M 8.112). Regarding the phrase "in the case of women": the meaning is that there is no fault in taking false oaths for the purpose of satisfying a woman in private; likewise for false oaths for the sake of purifying a marriage; likewise for false oaths for the purpose of feeding a cow; likewise for false oaths for the purpose of fuel for necessary oblations; and likewise for false oaths for the purpose of protecting Brāhmaṇas and others. Thus says Yama:
694. But by making a false oath involving the killing of an insect, a man becomes guilty both of falsehood and of slaughter. 695.
Therefore, a man should not take a false oath according to his own desire.

The term "insect" (*kīṭa*) is an illustration for any living being whatsoever. Therefore, the meaning is that when a false oath is made—such as "If this was done by me, then let there be the killing of a Brahmin for me"—the perpetrator incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).
Thus [ends the work] composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Harinārāyaṇa,
the younger brother of Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Hṛdayanārāyaṇa,
and the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Darpanārāyaṇa.
The Section on Procedure (*kriyāpāda*) in the *Vyavahāracintāmaṇi*. Now, the determination of the case (*nirṇaya*).
Regarding this, Vyāsa states:
"A decision is recorded as being of eight kinds: by means of proofs, by the conduct of the parties, by oath, by the king's command, or by the mutual agreement of the litigants. [Vy 1.1]
697. Written documents, witnesses, and possession are recorded as the threefold means of proof. The wise know inference to be the logical reason (*hetu*), and reasoning (*tarka*) as well.
698. Established local custom and ancient practice are declared to be *carita* (usage).
Oaths corresponding to the nature of the matter are recorded as the ordeal by truth, the balance, and so forth.

In their absence, the wise know that the decision rests upon the king’s command. (Vyavahāranirṇaya 1.3) By the term "by means of proofs" (*pramāṇaiḥ*), there is an intention to refer to each individually: written documents, witnesses, and possession. Reasoning (*tarka*) and inference (*anumāna*) constitute a single category as the basis for the cause. The phrase "the ordeal by truth, the balance, and so forth" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all divine ordeals; therefore, this constitutes the eightfold division. It should be noted that the word "oath" (*śapatha*) is used here in a figurative sense in accordance with the traditional classification.
In this regard, the procedure for determination in cases of oaths and ordeals is as follows;
therein Kātyāyana states:
"If, within fourteen days, there has been no misfortune caused by the king or by fate for the [accused]..."
A terrible calamity arises; he should be known as pure in his oath. "Calamity" (vyasana) means misfortune (āpad); "terrible" (ghora) means causing extreme affliction.
Viṣṇu [states this] regarding the administration of the treasury.
If, within fourteen days or even twenty-one days,
one should see illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or even a royal calamity,
one should know that person to be impure; conversely, in the opposite case, one should know them to be pure.
The Grandfather said:
"If an unnatural transformation is observed in anyone after three nights, seven nights, or even fourteen days, that person is a doer of evil. [Pi 161]
If that [misfortune] were to happen to that one person alone and not to all people,
then illness, fire, or the death of a kinsman would be the very means for his realization.
— Kātyāyana.
704. Now, regarding the failure of the ordeal: after three weeks, one should cause the accused to pay that amount with effort, as well as a fine equal to it. 705.
This applies if that [result] should happen to that single person and not to all people.
Disease, fire, the death of kinsmen, debt, and he shall pay a fine.
Fever, dysentery, boils, pain in the hidden bones,
eye disease, throat disease, and likewise insanity arise.

Headache and the breaking of the arms are divine afflictions for men. "Divine contradiction" refers to disease, the death of a kinsman, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that one person": this does not mean a plague or similar calamity that spreads across a region; rather, the meaning is that a disease or the like, arising immediately after an oath and unique to the accused, is the sign of defeat. Nārada, in the section on oaths, states:
707. If after two weeks (fourteen days) a very great abnormality occurs, he should not be targeted by a wise man, because the appointed time has elapsed.

Regarding this, Halāyudha states that the arrangement of three nights (*trirātra*) and so forth applies respectively to those who are Brāhmaṇas and the other castes. The Pārijāta states that the arrangement of three nights and so forth depends on the degree of intensity of the deity’s wrath once the water used for its ablution has been drunk. The Pradīpa states that if there is excellence due to the location and time, or if the object is formidable, it is three nights; as the excellence diminishes, the period becomes seven nights and so forth.

All of this, with the exception of the [ordeals] lasting seven or three nights and so forth, is common to oaths as well, because the requirement is the same. However, Kātyāyana states that if the defendant is victorious, the punishment falls upon the plaintiff alone:
"But for one who has been accused on the basis of a formal challenge and has been cleared by the *kośa* [ordeal], [the plaintiff is punished]."
The righteous king should cause the accuser to pay the legal fine for the accusation;
however, he should honor a man who has been cleared by ordeal.
Here, the terms "treasure" (*kośa*) and "ordeal" (*divya*) are illustrative; the intent is merely to indicate that the person has emerged victorious, as the logic applies equally to both.
Kātyāyana states the punishment for one who wins and one who loses:
"One who is pure should be made to pay fifty; one who is impure shall be subject to a fine.
Fifty means fifty *paṇas*.
He alone determines the punishment for failure.

710. In cases involving poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel (kośa), rice grains, the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka), and the divine ordeal, one should prescribe the punishment in due order. [K 460]

One should calculate a fine of one thousand, six hundred, five hundred, four, three, two, or even one *paṇa* for each successive lower offense; that is, for a minor offense, starting from one thousand *paṇas*. "In a minor case" refers to a case involving a transgression. "Starting from one thousand" refers to the *paṇas*.
Now, the relative strength and weakness of the means of decision.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Dharma (righteousness), vyavahāra (legal procedure), caritra (customary practice), and rājaśāsana (the king’s edict)..."
This fourfold legal procedure consists of the subsequent subverting the preceding.

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent subverts the preceding": in matters of dharma, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict, each subsequent one subverts each preceding one; this is the meaning. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
Having thoroughly investigated the matter and deliberated upon it with reason,
and having tested it through oaths,
the determination of dharma is to be known as that wherein the defendant admits the claim; that is the final decision.
Or, when it has been properly purified by divine means, that is declared to be the second.
This two-fold determination is called *dharmya* (in accordance with dharma). Furthermore—
715. Where a decision is made by relying solely upon the treatises (*śāstra*), that should be known as a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*); by means of that, the Dharma is set aside.
The meaning is that *dharma*—that which is called Dharma—is set aside, or rather sublated, by that decision known as a legal proceeding.
Kātyāyana states regarding the scope of sublation:
"But where an ordeal that is consistent with reason is excluded from a legal matter, there the Dharma is sublated by the judicial proceeding, and not otherwise. [K 39]
The meaning is that a decision dependent on inadmissible divine means is sublated by judicial procedure.
Bṛhaspati:
"When a decision is made based on local custom and the consensus of merchants, the legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) therein is sublated. [B 1.20]

The *naigamas* are city-dwellers and merchants. The connection is that [a decision] is reached by means of inference according to the consensus of the *naigamas*. The meaning is that by this decision known as *caritra* (established custom), the decision known as *vyavahāra* (legal procedure), which follows the general rules of the scriptures, is sublated. Kātyāyana states:
"But when a custom contrary to logic is established by kings..."

In this manner, conduct may be set aside there by the king's command. (K 42) 719. It has been declared that the rebuttal which subverts [the opponent's position] is according to this rule; where there is a subversion otherwise, there dharma is destroyed. (K 43)

"Contrary to justice" (*nyāyataḥ*)—the meaning is that whatever conduct is contrary to justice should be set aside by the king's command. Alternatively, *nyāyataḥ* is used with the suffix *tasi* functioning as all case endings; the meaning is that even where there is a conflict between two principles of justice or two legal treatises (*śāstra*), the legal proceeding is determined by the king's command. Now, regarding the matter to be decided: on this point, Nārada says:
Even if he has admitted the charge himself, or even if he has been caught in his own conduct,
or even if he has failed in his ritual duties, he deserves a formal determination by the assembly.
Once he has been so determined by them, he is subsequently to be punished by the king according to the legal treatises.

"Self-accused" means one who has admitted defeat for himself alone. "Convinced by his own conduct" means one whose defeat is determined by signs such as trembling, perspiration, and change of color due to agitation. "Defeated by the legal process" means one who has reached a state of exhaustion through the procedure, such as an ordeal (*divya*), and thus incurred defeat; that is to say, immediately thereafter he deserves the determination of the court members—that is, he deserves to be declared defeated by the court members acting together. Yājñavalkya (2.10):
"If he denies [the claim] and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the debt to the creditor and an equal amount to the king."
"One who brings a false accusation shall forfeit double the amount of the claim" (Yājñavalkya 2.11).
"In case of denial" means in case of concealment; "established" means made to admit it through witnesses and other means.
Manu says:
But when the debtor has been made to confess the debt through evidence,
the judge shall cause him to pay the amount to the creditor and a small fine according to his ability.
Whatever amount one denies, or whatever amount one falsely asserts, [he shall be compelled to pay that].

"Those two, being ignorant of the law, shall also be punished by the king with double that fine. (M 8.59) Regarding "one who denies" (*apavyayamānam*), this means one who conceals [the debt]. "By means of evidence" (*kāraṇena*) refers to the establishment of proof through witnesses and the like. The phrase "as much as" (*yāvat*) means: to whatever extent the debtor denies the amount, or for whatever sum the creditor falsely brings a claim, both of them—having engaged in the dispute due to the fault of their intention (*āśaya-doṣa*)—shall be made to pay a fine equal to twice the amount of wealth that was the subject of the dispute. This is the meaning. It should be understood that if the denial is due to forgetfulness and the like, rather than a fault of intention, they shall pay only a small portion of a fine according to their capacity.

In this matter, for one who denies a fine that is equal, double, or even a small fraction [of the value], a determination must be made based on caste, age, wealth, conduct, and so forth. Some maintain that the determination is made by taking into account the strength of the offender's intention and the strength of the victim's grievance. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the power, as well as the age, the occupation, and the wealth, the king shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (YDh 1.368)
Bṛhaspati also states:
"And in this case, a punishment corresponding to the offense has been prescribed.
Vyāsa says that the "punishment for the sake of wealth" refers to the punishment intended for one who denies the debt beyond what was admitted by the defendant who offers a confession as a reply.

"But when a litigant denies [a charge] and then admits it himself, that is to be known as an admission; for such a case, half the fine is prescribed. [Vyavahāranirṇaya 1.115] Nārada states the punishment for a Śūdra who falsely accuses members of the twice-born castes:
728. Those Śūdras who bring false accusations against Brāhmaṇas shall have their tongues cut out and be impaled upon a stake by the king. 729.
One who denies a document that has been presented, even if only one part of it is proven, [is liable for punishment].

The debtor shall be made to pay all the amounts by the king, but he must not be made to pay what was not previously declared. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.20) When a creditor has caused a document to be written for several items—such as gold, silver, copper, and so forth—stating, "You owe me these," and the accused denies everything, yet even a single portion such as gold or silver is proven by witnesses and other means, then the defendant must be made to pay to the plaintiff the entire amount that was the subject of the claim. Halāyudha explains that the meaning of this is: after one part has been proven, even if the matter was not raised at the time of the formal statement (*bhāṣā*), it shall not be made payable from the side of the defendant if it was not presented then.
Nārada:
But when there is a charge involving multiple matters,
if the defendant denies all the points yet one part is proven, it is proper that even that [admitted portion] be granted.

Both of these [rules] are intended for those matters that are mutually inseparable (*avinābhāva*), because they are rooted in logic (*nyāyamūlaka*). Alternatively, this refers to the subject matter of a lawsuit involving a wager (*sapaṇavivāda*), wherein one says, "I shall give everything once even a single part has been proven. To this effect, Yājñavalkya says:
"If a lawsuit should be accompanied by a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine, his own wager, and the debt itself to the creditor. (YDh 2.18)
"One's own wager" means a wager made by oneself. Now follows the procedure for acknowledging victory; regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Because he maintains his initial claim, because he honors the presiding judge and others,
and because he receives the document of victory, one is declared a victor in the world.
— Kātyāyana.
The king, having first shown him respect, should join the proponent with the proven matter and give him a written document containing that matter.
Likewise—
734. Whatever has been rejected or written down, that the member of the court (*sabhyo*) shall destroy; likewise, even a subsequent plea (*paścātkāra*) shall undoubtedly be set aside. 735.
Where a legal action (*kriyā*) has been rejected by the plaintiff himself through a means of proof (*pramāṇa*), [it is void].

In that case, a *paścātkāra* (post-judgment) may occur; it is not prescribed in all cases. When slaves, women, land, houses, gardens, or scribes are defeated, the king should always grant a *paścātkāra* in these very instances.

*Paścātkāra* is the action taken after the decision, such as the document of victory (*jayapatra*) and so forth. *Pramāṇa* refers to witnesses and other means of proof. The phrase "in these very cases" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), because learned men provide such documents even in other circumstances.
Now, furthermore, regarding legal procedure (*nyāya*): Manu says:
Whatever has been adjudicated and whatever instruction has been given, wherever it may have occurred, one should know that to be established according to dharma; one must not reverse it again.

"Decided" (*tīritam*)—this is the form of the root *tṛ* (meaning "to cross over" or "to complete") belonging to the *curādi* class, in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form. Thus, the meaning is "concluded after having reached a definitive decision. "Instructed" (*anuśiṣṭam*) means "declared by witnesses. "In any [court]," such as an assembly in a village or elsewhere. This, however, is the natural interpretation of Lakṣmīdhara and others. In another text, however, it is stated: "Only when witnesses and the like are found to be corrupt; otherwise, there is no 'deciding' or 'instructing' of what has been deliberated. To that effect, Kātyāyana says: 738.
That side which is determined by the members of the court as being "untrue" or "true,"...

"That case is declared to be 'decided' (tīrita) when it has been adjudicated (anuśiṣṭa) due to the wickedness of the witnesses. However, where the losing party, considering even a decision and an adjudication to have been made contrary to dharma, raises an objection again, Nārada states that a trial by legal procedure must indeed be conducted once more for him, who is to be fined double the amount of the subject of the dispute he had accepted:
"Whoever considers a decision or an adjudication to have been made contrary to dharma..."

"Having imposed a double fine, he should overturn that decision again. [NMā 1.65] This refers to the various ways in which a decision may be made contrary to the Dharma. He himself also states that when a matter has been concluded by one's own action, there is no further recourse to the examination of justice.

In the case of witnesses, members of the court, or assessors who have been dismissed due to being found defective, there is a rule for a renewed examination; however, for those who have reached a conclusion through their own conduct, there is no provision for a second trial.

The meaning is that "review" (*punardarśana*) refers to the re-examination of witnesses and assessors who have reached a state of exhaustion through the testimony of the witnesses and the deliberation of the assessors; that is, the presentation of the legal argument once again. "Upon refutation" (*dūṣaṇe*) means when there is a refutation of both the witnesses and the assessors. "Those exhausted by their own conduct" (*svacaryāvasitānām*) refers to those who have reached a state of exhaustion because they have themselves admitted defeat through their own actions, such as speaking in contradiction to one another. "There is no rule for a second birth" (*nāsti paunarbhavo vidhiḥ*) means that there is no further proceeding of the lawsuit. On this very point, Bṛhaspati says:

741. Because fleeing is not a valid defense and because one relies on the position of another, the lawsuit of the defeated party is upheld, but not that of one who has been defeated by his own words alone.

This is what is brought forward here: even if a decision has been reached according to the law by faultless witnesses, jurors, and others, it must not be reconsidered simply because the litigant wishes to alter it; for if it were, there would be the consequence of endless instability, contradicting the statement of Manu: "What has been decided and what has been adjudicated [must stand]."

However, when a case has been decided by corrupt witnesses or assessors due to greed, negligence, or other such motives, it must indeed be re-examined once the corruption is established by evidence. As Yājñavalkya says:
"But when lawsuits have been wrongly decided, the assessors, together with the judges, shall be fined by the king twice the amount of the dispute. (YDh 2.305)
Nārada also says:
"But that which is seen without witnesses and decided by an improper path, or seen by those whose minds are not in agreement, deserves to be reviewed again. [NQ 1.14]
Likewise:
744. Having reached a decision together with many Brahmins who have mastered the scriptures, he should punish the former members of the court along with the victorious party if they are found guilty.
By the term "members of the court" (*sabhyān*), witnesses (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) are also implied.
Yājñavalkya also states: "One should annul legal proceedings brought about by force or fraud. (YDh 2.31ab)

Furthermore, when a plaintiff who has been defeated—having raised a defect that was difficult for the witnesses, assessors, and others to perceive despite it having been determined—is unwilling to accept the decision but instead requests a retrial, the judge should impose a double fine and investigate the alleged defect only superficially at first. Once the defect is established, the double fine should be waived and the case on the points of dispute should proceed again according to the truth. "But when lawsuits have been wrongly decided, they should be reviewed again by the king. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.305ab)

Thus, by the very force of the text as written by Yājñavalkya, the refutation is established. However, in the alternative view where the refutation is admitted by the disputant, the assessors (*sabhyas*) must be made to pay double the fine, because it is the duty of the king to prevent over-extension (*atiprasakti*). As Nārada says: "In a wrongly decided lawsuit, the assessors shall incur that same fine;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path [of justice] without punishment. [NMā 1.66]

The meaning of the phrase "he should overturn that decision" is that, having investigated in truth the defects of the defeated witnesses, assessors, and so forth, he should initiate the legal proceeding anew. This is logical; for when the verdict (*tīrita*) and the subsequent instruction (*anuśiṣṭi*) are rendered by the assessors and witnesses, their invalidity depends solely upon the defects of those very individuals, and not otherwise. Therefore, a determination of the true facts (*tattvanirūpaṇa*) alone is appropriate.
Yājñavalkya (7.48): "He who, though defeated according to justice, thinks 'I am not defeated'..."

"But having won again in the assembly, he shall cause [the loser] to pay double the fine" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.306). The meaning is this: even though one has been defeated according to the facts, if—suspecting a defect in the substantive witnesses and so forth, and considering the trial to have been improper—he determines that defect to be non-existent after investigation, he should be made to pay a fine of double the amount of the wealth in dispute from that legal matter. However, if the minister or the judge themselves are corrupt, the fine is not double; rather, Manu states it is one thousand [paṇas].
749. Ministers or judges who should decide a case otherwise than it ought to be decided, the king himself shall decide that case and cause them to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas].—
One thousand paṇas.
"Two hundred *paṇas*," according to the statement of Viṣṇu [Vi 4.14a].

Thus, this is the summary: when there is a suspicion that the previous deliberation was incorrect, a new deliberation takes place. In that case as well, the defeated party must first accept double the fine. Then, once the new deliberation proceeds, if he fulfills the defects of witnesses and so forth that he himself previously alleged, the punishment shall be for the witnesses and others alone, and there shall be a renewed deliberation of the subject of the dispute. However, if he does not fulfill them, the punishment falls upon the defeated party alone, and there is no further deliberation.
Now, regarding the withdrawal [of false testimony],
Manu says:
"In whatever lawsuit false testimony has been given..."
That particular transaction shall be rescinded; even what has been performed shall be as if unperformed.
(M 8.117) 752. A fraudulent mortgage or sale, a fraudulent gift or acceptance, or any transaction where one perceives fraud—such a transaction he shall annul. (M 8.165)

"Yoga" means fraud (*upadhi*). The meaning is that the king shall annul whatever has been done by means of that [fraud], such as the pledging of property and so forth. "Fraud" (*upadhi*) refers to deception. Here, "pledging" (*ādhamana*) and the like are merely illustrative; other [acts] as well are to be annulled. Halāyudha says: "Yoga is the destruction of trust; the meaning is that he shall annul sales and other transactions effected through that [fraud]. Likewise:
753. "Whatever is given by force, whatever is enjoyed by force, and whatever is caused to be written by force—Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be null and void.
— Nārada.
754. "A legal transaction (vyavahāra) that has been concluded with women, at night, outside the village, within a house, or with enemies—even if already finalized—must be performed again.
Likewise:

755. Even if a statement is established, it does not constitute truth if it speaks of matters external to the fixed rules of worldly convention. [NMā 2.15] That speech which is said to concern a subject matter outside the fixed rules of worldly convention is not true, even if it is established and supported by means of proof such as written documents. Whatever matter is established by such speech is not to be carried out—for example, when someone sues another who has sons and so forth, saying, "He gave me his entire estate," and so on.
Manu: A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, or under another's control, or by a child, an elderly person, or one who is unconnected [to the matter], is not valid.
A slave is one who is under another's absolute control; an unauthorized person is one who is not related [to the transaction].
Yājñavalkya (7.57): One should annul legal transactions brought about through force or fraud.
[One should avoid] women, the interior of the house, and those [offenses] committed by enemies outside; likewise, "outside" means from a place appropriate for public business. Nārada says:
Whatever action a child performs, or likewise one who is not his own master,
even that they declare to be "not done" in the treatises, according to those people who know the treatises.
For even an independent person, if he performs an action while having fallen from his natural state, [it is considered invalid].
They say that even such an act is indeed unperformed, for he is not independent due to those causes.
Those who are overcome by desire and anger, afflicted by fear and calamity,
and enveloped by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen into an unnatural state.

761. Likewise, an act performed by a slave is declared to be as if unperformed, except by the master’s command; for a slave has no authority over himself. 762. And an act performed by a son against the will of the father is likewise considered unperformed.
They say that even such a person is as if not born at all; a slave and a son are equal in this regard.

Because the term "dependent" (*asvatantra*) was already mentioned, the repetition of the word "minor" (*bāla*)—even though the minor has already been included—is for the purpose of establishing the minor’s lack of independence even in the absence of both parents. Furthermore, this refers to matters other than the maintenance of the family, since the subsequent statement says, "even one dependent on another [is independent] for the sake of the family.
*Prakṛti* means nature or inherent disposition. *Aprakṛtiṃ gataḥ* means being situated outside of one's nature.
"Without the father's consent" means having removed the father's *chanda*, which is to say his desire or wish. Kātyāyana [states]:
"There shall be no giving, mortgaging, or selling of fields, houses, or slaves."
Those performed without independence shall not attain success, even if they are described; "not described" means not approved by one who is independent—this is the ellipsis. Thus says Nārada.
They say that transactions entered into by a woman are not valid when there is no distress,
especially those concerning the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field.
These very transactions are valid if the husband gives his consent.
In the absence of a husband, the son; or in the absence of both husband and son, the king [is the authority].

(N 1.27) 766. An act performed by one who is the eldest in the family, or the most excellent, or who is established in his natural state, is considered truly done; that which is done by one who is not independent is not considered done. (N 1.42)

By the phrase "in times of distress" (*anāpadi*), it is stated that even those [authorities] established by women are indeed authoritative for the purpose of remedying such distress. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of husband and son," the term "son" (*putra*) also includes the son of a co-wife (*sapatnīputra*). Therefore, it should be understood that in their absence, the king is the authority.
Now, the definition of independent and dependent [authority]:
regarding this, Nārada says:
767. Sovereignty, however, is traditionally held to belong to the eldest; seniority is determined by virtue and age.
Likewise— 768. All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent.
A disciple is traditionally held to be dependent, while independence resides in the teacher.
[N 1.33] 769 All women, sons, slaves, and dependents are dependent; however, the householder who inherits it in due order is independent therein. [N 1.34]
A child should be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
a boy is called a *bāla* until the sixteenth year, and he is also termed a *pogaṇḍa*. Beyond that age, he is knowledgeable in legal affairs and independent, except in relation to his parents.
As long as they both live, he shall not be independent, even if he is advanced in years.
Of those two, the father is superior because of the preeminence of the seed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother; and in her absence, the elder brother.
Of those two parents.

And this demonstration of independence and dependence is intended to establish that even an act performed by one who is dependent—without the consent of the independent [parent]—must be rescinded by the king; it is not for the sake of some unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because Nārada specifically mentions the "clause for the rescission of what has been done. He clarifies this very point:
"All these are always independent among those who are dependent."
"In matters of instruction, distribution, and sale, they are considered masters.
[N 1.38] These refer to the previously mentioned persons beginning with the king.

And because of the statement "in their absence, the elder brother," it should be understood that in the phrase "excepting the parents," this implies even in the absence of the elder brother and the others.

Although it has been established by the statement "in the absence of the seed-owner [the mother is the authority]" that the mother possesses independence while the son lacks it, nevertheless—on the basis of Nārada’s own intent in the phrase "in the absence of the husband"—any transaction performed during non-distress times by an independent mother without the consent of her son, even if he is not himself independent, must indeed be annulled. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the son’s consent would serve only an invisible (transcendental) purpose; for since the father's wealth passes to the son in his absence, the consent of the son can well have a visible (worldly) purpose. Śaṅkha and Likhita:
774. Those who have a father are not independent.
While the grandfather is alive, the father’s dependence is like that of a son. Consequently, an action performed by the father succeeds only with the grandfather’s consent, and not otherwise.
Kātyāyana states that even the youngest brother is dependent upon the eldest as long as their wealth is undivided, but not so when the wealth is divided.
A father who lacks independence, one who has a father, a brother, or even a brother’s son;
likewise, a younger sibling who has not yet divided his property, a slave, and a laborer.
— Hārīta.
Whether for the purpose of giving, or for the purpose of wealth, or especially for the purpose of dharma;
whether in taking or in spending, a woman does not deserve independence.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that even when she is not independent in some particular matter, she is still an authority.
All of these are authoritative in the buying and selling of commodities,
provided they have previously engaged in such transactions and their authority has been consented to.
In the same way, for fields and other property, the brother, the brother’s son, and the son may act as authorities.
If they have been authorized by their master to perform a specific task while departing,
he who has been authorized for a particular matter is indeed the master in that matter;
as its owner, he is not entitled to act otherwise than what was performed by him.
Bṛhaspati explains the one with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*):
"He who is appointed by his master over the management of income and expenditure, as well as in lending at interest, agriculture, and trade, is known as one with full authority. [B 9.29]
The master shall not contradict any transaction made by him, whether it concerns gain or loss, expenditure or income,
whether occurring in his own country or abroad.
— Manu.

Even one who is dependent for the sake of the family may conduct legal business, whether in his own country or abroad; the superior shall not obstruct him. (M 8.167) "Dependent" (*adhyadhīna*) means one who is under the control of another, such as a son, a slave, and so forth. "May conduct" (*samācaret*) means he may perform it. The sense is that even in such a matter, there is no requirement for the consent of the master. "The superior" (*jyāyān*) refers to the independent person, such as a father and so forth.
Kātyāyana says:
A father has authority over his son’s sons and daughters-in-law regarding instruction, as well as regarding sale and gift; however, he has no authority over his own son regarding sale or gift.

Regarding this—some maintain that the statement in Nārada’s work, “In instruction, in giving away, and in selling, [the parents] are considered masters,” which establishes authority over giving and selling, refers specifically to the giving and selling of a son as such; therefore, there is no contradiction. According to the traditional view (saṃpradāya), the father has authority over the giving and so forth of the son with the son’s consent, but lacks authority without his consent.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Harinārāyaṇa,
the younger brother of Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Hṛdayanārāyaṇa,
and the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Darpanārāyaṇa.
The Section on Decision in the *Vyavahāracintāmaṇi*.
Thus [ends] the work composed by the Great Teacher, the Venerable Sanmiśra Śrī Vācaspati.
The Vyavahāracintāmaṇi is complete.
